entries.title: Prosecutors Say Probe Into Ilhan Omar Goes Back to the 1980s
entries.summary: Newly unsealed court records center on a fight over sensitive legislative records in the raid of Omar’s Washington home.
entries.content:
A federal judge on Monday unsealed some records connected to the Trump administration’s ongoing investigation into Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar for alleged immigration fraud, much of it dealing with a fight over constitutional questions about the search of the congresswoman’s Washington home.

While most of the 169 pages unsealed are heavily redacted, at least one shows prosecutors say their investigation looks back to Omar in the 1980s when she was a child.

In seeking a warrant to raid Omar’s Washington home, prosecutors clashed with U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew J. Sharbaugh over protections for the congresswoman’s sensitive legislative records days before agents showed up in the early-morning hours at her house, the newly released records show. Justice Department attorneys then sought to keep Sharbaugh’s criticism sealed.

Neither Omar nor any of her family members have been charged in connection with the investigation, though several of her relatives have received grand jury subpoenas from the Justice Department.

The dispute revealed in the documents centers on the Constitution’s Speech and Debate Clause, which protects Congress from interference by the executive branch. The Justice Department argued that because the investigation concerned Omar’s private life, it did not need to follow special search procedures for her congressional files.

Sharbaugh disagreed. On Oct. 9, he ordered prosecutors to add extra safeguards, giving Omar a chance to identify congressionally related materials before the Oct. 12 raid.

“No matter how small the potential volume of legislative materials at issue, the constitutional protections remain,” Sharbaugh wrote on Oct. 15, adding that prosecutors failed to revise their plans in response to his concerns. “Instead, it stood pat on its existing proposed search protocols without further modification.”

The documents released also included a supplemental brief — prepared by the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro — supporting the request for a warrant to search Omar’s Washington residence.

The brief reveals that the government applied for the warrant on Oct. 2, 10 days before Homeland Security Investigations agents raided Omar’s D.C. home and seized 17 items including cell phones, laptops and passports.

Prosecutors claimed they had “a rock-solid basis to issue the warrant,” describing alleged violations involving Omar "occurring between 1980 and the present.”

Three days after the raid, Sharbaugh moved to release his explanation of the dispute over federal search procedures.

The Justice Department objected, calling his account “an incomplete and flawed summary of what occurred,” according to the unsealed records.

“The United States believes ILHAN has committed (redacted) crimes over decades — beginning long before she was ever in Congress,” Pirro wrote in her arguments against unsealing the court records.

More than half of pages in the release are completely or heavily redacted, including several pages with the label “Special Search Procedures” — the revised procedures Sharbaugh ordered the DOJ to prepare. The 67-page affidavit laying out the government’s evidence also remains sealed.

The entire case has been under seal since federal authorities raided Omar’s D.C. home last month, but a coalition of news organizations, including The Washington Sun, filed to unseal the records. The Justice Department has argued against releasing them, telling the federal court it could jeopardize the criminal investigation into Omar.

“How a search warrant was executed—including what was seized and anything Ms. Omar said or admitted during the search—are precisely the sort of highly sensitive facts that shouldn’t be made public during an ongoing investigation that has yet to yield a charging decision,” Pirro argued.

James Boasberg, the chief judge of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, considered the news organizations’ applications in a hearing Tuesday. While he agreed that a “vast majority” of the search warrant should remain sealed, Boasberg questioned why information about any efforts to safeguard Omar’s constitutional rights through the course of the investigation should be kept confidential.

During the hearing, Boasberg ordered the Justice Department to submit a redaction proposal by Friday for the court to consider before releasing the documents Monday. The judge also appeared skeptical of the DOJ’s argument that its search warrant records should not be released because it had not been fully completed — even though the warrant had been returned to the magistrate judge, a common practice when executing such orders.

After the raid, the Minnesota congresswoman immediately characterized the operation as an “outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies” in a post on X.

Omar was born in Somalia, but she and her family fled the country after a civil war began there in 1991. She became a U.S. citizen in 2000. The HSI raid was part of a probe into potential immigration fraud and questions about citizenship paperwork Omar’s late father prepared in 1995.

President Donald Trump’s top immigration officials have continued to speak publicly about the substantial evidence the government allegedly has to support the investigation into Omar. White House border czar Tom Homan said after the raid that he had been told that HSI has “a strong case,” while Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin described the evidence against Omar as “strong.”

Trump has said he had “nothing to do” with the investigation, but he has repeatedly called for Omar to resign from Congress — alleging she used a “fake” name when she was sworn in. A spokesperson from Omar’s office pushed back against the statements last month, calling them “flat out false.”

This story has been updated with further information from the unsealed documents.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin, Gavin J. Quinton

entries.title: The Commanders Make a Little Magic in a 22-20 Win Over the Bengals
entries.summary: A frenzied final drive led to a game-winning field goal as Washington upset red-hot Cincinnati.
entries.content:
There has been near-constant chatter this season about the Commanders' need for receiver help. It started in the offseason and only grew louder when veteran Terry McLaurin went down with an injury in Week 6.

As it turns out, Washington may have had the solution on its roster this whole time.

Late on Monday night, rookie Antonio Williams hauled in a 42-yard pass with the clock ticking down, capping a sterling 122-yard performance and giving his team a short field goal attempt to win a game that had seemed lost just seconds before. Drew Stevens nailed that 26-yarder and the Commanders beat the seemingly unbeatable Bengals, 22-20.

"I personally live for those moments — high pressure situations," quarterback Jayden Daniels said. "You want to go out there and make your mark on the game."

https://x.com/NFL/status/2125081616204599547
The win was made possible on defense, where Washington limited the league's hottest offense to a modest output. Ja'Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, the Bengals' star wideouts, combined for just 74 yards.

Up front, defensive coordinator Daronte Jones decided he would blitz, blitz again and blitz some more. The Commanders hit Joe Burrow 10 times and sacked him three times, keeping pressure on the MVP candidate and forcing him into quick, short throws. Outside of a 31-yard touchdown to Higgins in the second quarter, the defensive backs — led by replacement starter Rasul Douglas — limited game-changing plays.

The Commanders' offense took a little while to get going. High snaps, blown assignments and an inability to stop Cincinnati linebacker Boye Mafe (three sacks) hampered the unit throughout the first half. Washington went into the break with just one third-down conversion. At one point, receiver Stefon Diggs was seen on the broadcast yelling in frustration on the sideline.

But maybe there’s a method to Diggs’ madness, because after gaining just 28 net yards through the first 28 minutes of the game, the Commanders' offense went on a nine-play, 79-yard drive at the end of the first half to get on the board and cut the score to 10-7.

The momentum of that drive carried over into the first few minutes of the second half, when Daniels broke off a 47-yard scramble to set up a game-tying field goal.

But Washington was never able to pull away, and Cincinnati took a 20-19 lead on a 56-yard field goal from Evan McPherson with 46 seconds left. Washington got the ball back with no timeouts remaining and little reason to believe in its comeback chances.

Williams started the frenzied final drive with a 21-yard grab. After a spike, Daniels (289 yards passing and 55 yards rushing) targeted the rookie out of Clemson again, hitting him over the middle of the field. Williams sprinted down into the red zone, setting up Stevens' short, game-winning kick.

https://x.com/NFL/status/2125081931981209908
"To see those guys come through at the end, I thought that was one of our best team wins," coach Dan Quinn said.

The Commanders (4-5-1) scored their first consecutive wins since the 2024 playoffs, and things are now looking up: Their next two opponents, the Cardinals and Titans, have just four wins between them.
